blocks.text: Routing prompts classify an incoming request and direct it to the appropriate specialized assistant or handler, a different decision than tool selection, covered in the previous topic, which chooses among tools within a single agent already working on a task.

This topic covers how routing differs from tool selection, classifying requests into categories, routing to specialized assistants defined by their own role, handling genuinely ambiguous requests, and building a fallback route for requests that do not clearly fit anywhere.

A routing prompt looks at an incoming request and decides which specialized assistant, model, or workflow should actually handle it, this decision typically happens before any specific task execution begins, at the very front of a system handling varied requests.

Tool selection, covered in the previous topic, happens within an agent already working on a defined task, choosing which specific tool serves the current step, routing happens earlier and at a higher level, deciding which entire assistant or workflow should handle a request in the first place.

blocks.text: 3. Classifying an Incoming Request Into a Category

blocks.alt: Classifying an Incoming Request Into a Category

blocks.text: The first step in routing is classification, determining which predefined category a request actually belongs to, a billing question, a technical issue, a general inquiry, this connects directly to classification techniques covered in the earlier Prompt Iteration and Structured Outputs modules.

code.content:
categories = ["billing", "technical_support", "general_inquiry"]
prompt = (
    f"Classify this request into exactly one category: {categories}. "
    f"Request: {user_message}"
)

blocks.text: This connects directly to role definition and multi-agent prompting, both covered in earlier modules, each destination an incoming request can be routed to is typically a specialized assistant with its own clear role definition, exactly the job description concept covered earlier, tuned specifically for that category of request.

Not every request classifies cleanly, a billing question that also touches on a technical issue genuinely spans two categories, a routing prompt needs explicit guidance for this case, route to the primary concern, or route to a general assistant capable of bridging both, rather than forcing an artificially confident single category choice.
6. A Fallback Route for Unclassifiable Requests

blocks.alt: A Fallback Route for Unclassifiable Requests

blocks.text: A request that genuinely does not fit any defined category needs an explicit fallback route, a general purpose assistant capable of handling anything the specialized categories do not cover, rather than being forced into an ill fitting category simply because the routing system has no other option.

blocks.title: This mirrors the exclusion clause covered in the earlier Role Definition topic
blocks.content: Just as a well defined role states what falls explicitly outside its scope, a well designed routing system needs an explicit answer for what happens to a request that falls outside every defined category.

blocks.text: For a routing decision the model is not confident about, rather than silently routing to a possibly wrong category, a well designed system can route low confidence classifications to human review, or to a general assistant capable of asking a clarifying question, treating routing confidence itself as a signal worth acting on.

A message asking "why was I charged twice and also my app keeps crashing" genuinely spans both billing and technical categories, a well designed routing prompt recognizes this and either routes to a general assistant capable of addressing both, or explicitly splits the request into two separate routed sub-requests.

This connects to the metric-driven iteration process covered in an earlier module, testing a routing prompt against a genuinely varied, realistic set of requests, including ambiguous and edge case ones, not just clean, obviously categorizable examples, reveals whether the routing logic actually holds up in practice.

A team building a customer support system initially routes requests using only three narrow categories, testing against real historical support messages reveals about fifteen percent of requests do not cleanly fit any of them, and were previously being forced into a poorly matching category.

Adding an explicit general inquiry fallback category, along with guidance for genuinely ambiguous multi-category requests, brings routing accuracy up substantially on the same test set, since requests that do not cleanly fit a specific category no longer get forced into the wrong one.

items: Defining only narrow categories with no fallback route for requests that do not clearly fit any of them
Forcing a genuinely ambiguous, multi-category request into a single artificial category choice
Confusing routing, which chooses a handler for an entire incoming request, with tool selection within an already assigned task
Testing routing only against clean, obviously categorizable examples instead of genuinely varied, ambiguous real requests

blocks.text: Define three specialized categories for a domain you are familiar with, write a routing prompt with an explicit fallback category, and test it against five realistic requests including at least one that genuinely spans two categories.

Routing prompts classify an incoming request and direct it to the appropriate specialized assistant, a higher level decision than tool selection within an already assigned task, requiring explicit handling for genuinely ambiguous requests and a fallback route for anything that does not fit a defined category, validated against realistic, varied test requests.
